summary: Describes an enhancement to OSPF that lets a router stay on the forwarding path while its OSPF software restarts. This is sometimes called graceful restart or non-stop forwarding. If the topology changes during the restart, the procedure automatically reverts to a normal restart to avoid routing loops.

plainLanguage.summary: Graceful OSPF Restart lets a router restart its routing software without dropping the traffic it is carrying. Before the restart the router tells its neighbours that it is going away for a while, and they keep sending traffic to it instead of routing around it. The arrangement ends by itself if the network changes, if the router takes too long, or if a neighbour does not support it.

questions: how does ospf restart without dropping traffic
what is non-stop forwarding in ospf
subtitle: A router restarts its OSPF software and keeps forwarding traffic, with neighbours holding the route open for it.

tldr.problem: OSPF normally routes around a router whose software restarts, because the router's link-state database is briefly out of date and the alternative risks routing loops and black holes.
tldr.mechanism: The restarting router announces a grace-LSA naming a grace period, and its neighbours keep advertising it as fully adjacent for that time, as long as the topology does not change.
tldr.outcome: The procedure reverts to a normal OSPF restart by itself when the topology changes, when the grace period ends, or when a neighbour does not support the enhancement, so an unmodified network behaves exactly as before.

today: RFC 3623 is a Proposed Standard on the Internet standards track, and no RFC in the site index obsoletes or updates it. It extends OSPF version 2 as specified in RFC 2328, and its Appendix A defines the grace-LSA used by the procedure.

sections.title: Why OSPF Needs Graceful Restart
sections.content:
Many Internet routers implement a separation of control and forwarding functions. Certain processors are dedicated to control and management tasks such as OSPF routing, while other processors perform the data forwarding tasks. That separation creates the possibility of maintaining a router's data forwarding capability while the router's control software is restarted or reloaded, which this RFC calls graceful restart or non-stop forwarding.

OSPF presents a problem to that idea. Under normal operation OSPF intentionally routes around a restarting router while it rebuilds its link-state database, because the restarting router's database is briefly out of date. The neighbours achieve this by reissuing their LSAs with links to the restarting router omitted. The RFC says this avoidance is deliberate: it minimises the possibility of routing loops and black holes caused by a lack of database synchronisation.

That behaviour becomes wasteful when two conditions hold together: the network topology remains stable, and the restarting router is able to keep its forwarding tables across the restart. It is then safe to keep the restarting router on the forwarding path. This RFC documents the OSPF enhancements that make such a graceful restart possible, and automatically reverts to a standard OSPF restart for safety when topology changes are detected, or when one or more of the restarting router's neighbours do not support the enhancements.
sections.plainLanguage: Some routers run their routing software on a separate processor from the one that forwards traffic. This RFC lets such a router restart its routing software and keep forwarding traffic while it does. Neighbours normally route around a restarting router; with these changes they hold on to it for a while, as long as the network has not changed.

sections.title: The Restarting Router During the Grace Period
sections.content:
The period between the restart and the re-establishment of all adjacencies is the graceful restart itself. During it, the restarting router, which the RFC calls Router X, behaves in three specific ways.

  • It does not originate LSAs with LS types 1 to 5 and 7. It wants the other routers in the OSPF domain to calculate routes using the LSAs it originated prior to the restart. During this time it does not modify or flush received self-originated LSAs, and in particular the grace-LSAs it originated before the restart are left in place.
  • It runs its OSPF routing calculations, as specified in section 16 of RFC 2328. This is necessary to return any OSPF virtual links to operation. It does not install OSPF routes into the system's forwarding tables and relies on the forwarding entries it installed prior to the restart.
  • If it was the Designated Router on a given segment prior to the restart, it elects itself as the Designated Router again. It knows that it was the Designated Router because, while the associated interface is in the Waiting state, it receives a Hello packet from a neighbour listing it as the Designated Router.

Otherwise the restarting router operates the same as any other OSPF router. It discovers neighbours using the Hello protocol, elects Designated and Backup Designated Routers, performs the Database Exchange procedure to initially synchronise link-state databases with its neighbours, and maintains this synchronisation through flooding.
sections.plainLanguage: While it restarts, the router keeps quiet about its own links, so that its neighbours keep using the routes they already learned from it. It still runs its routing calculations so that virtual links come back, but it does not install new forwarding entries and relies on the ones it had before the restart.

sections.title: Entering Graceful Restart
sections.content:
The router is informed of the desire for its graceful restart when an appropriate command is issued by the network operator. The operator may also specify the length of the grace period, or the necessary grace period may be calculated by the router's OSPF software. In order to avoid the restarting router's LSAs from ageing out, the grace period should not exceed LSRefreshTime, which is 1800 seconds.

In preparation, Router X must make sure its forwarding tables are up to date and will remain in place across the restart. Common OSPF shutdown procedures are deliberately not performed, because the other OSPF routers are meant to act as if Router X remains in continuous service; for example Router X does not flush its locally originated LSAs, since they should remain in other routers' link-state databases throughout the restart period.

The router may also need to preserve the cryptographic sequence numbers used on each interface in non-volatile storage. An alternative is to use the router's clock for cryptographic sequence number generation and ensure that the clock is preserved across restarts, on the same or a redundant route processor. If neither can be guaranteed, it can take up to RouterDeadInterval seconds after the restart before adjacencies can be re-established, and that would force the grace period to be lengthened greatly.

Router X then originates the grace-LSAs, which are link-local Opaque-LSAs, one for each of its OSPF interfaces. Their LS age field is set to 0 and the requested grace period in seconds is inserted into the body. To make sure its neighbours receive them, the router should retransmit the grace-LSAs until they are acknowledged, using standard OSPF reliable flooding. If one or more fully adjacent neighbours do not receive the grace-LSAs, they will more than likely cause premature termination of the graceful restart. After the grace-LSAs have been sent, the router stores the fact that it is performing a graceful restart along with the length of the requested grace period in non-volatile storage. The RFC suggests that it may be easiest to store the absolute time of the end of the grace period.

Appendix B lists the parameters an implementation can configure. RestartSupport gives the router's level of support, with the values none, planned restart only, and planned/unplanned. RestartInterval is the graceful restart interval in seconds, with a range from 1 to 1800 seconds and a suggested default of 120 seconds.
sections.plainLanguage: An operator tells the router to restart gracefully, usually before a planned software reload. Before the restart the router checks that its forwarding tables are current and will survive, and it announces the planned restart to its neighbours with a special message. The announced grace period should not be longer than 1800 seconds, the time after which the router's own link-state advertisements would age out.

sections.title: When Graceful Restart Ends
sections.content:
Router X exits graceful restart when any of three things happens.

  • It has re-established all its adjacencies. It can determine this by examining the router-LSAs it last originated before the restart, and the pre-restart network-LSAs on the segments where it is the Designated Router. Those LSAs will have been received from the helping neighbours, and need not have been stored in non-volatile storage across the restart.
  • It receives an LSA that is inconsistent with its pre-restart router-LSA. For example, it receives a router-LSA originated by router Y that does not contain a link to X, even though X's pre-restart router-LSA did contain a link to Y. This indicates that Y does not support graceful restart, that Y never received the grace-LSA, or that Y has terminated its helper mode for some reason. A special case of LSA inconsistency is when Router X establishes an adjacency with router Y and does not receive an instance of its own pre-restart router LSA.
  • The grace period expires.

On exit, whether it succeeded or not, the router reverts to completely normal OSPF operation. It reoriginates its router-LSAs for all attached areas so that they have the correct contents, reoriginates network-LSAs on all segments where it is the Designated Router, and reruns its OSPF routing calculations, this time installing the results into the system forwarding table and originating summary-LSAs, Type-7 LSAs and AS-external-LSAs as necessary. It removes any remnant entries in the forwarding table that were installed before the restart but are no longer valid, flushes any received self-originated LSAs that are no longer valid, and flushes the grace-LSAs it originated.
sections.plainLanguage: The graceful restart ends when the router has its adjacencies back, when a neighbour's advertisements no longer match what the router had before the restart, or when the grace period runs out. The router then goes back to normal: it republishes its own link-state information, installs the routes it has calculated, and clears out anything left over from before the restart.

sections.title: The Helper Neighbor
sections.content:
The helper relationship is per network segment. As a helper neighbour for a restarting router X on a segment, router Y has two duties. It monitors the network for topology changes, and as long as there are none it continues to advertise its LSAs as if X had remained in continuous OSPF operation, so its LSAs keep listing an adjacency to X over that segment regardless of the adjacency's current synchronisation state. When helping over a virtual link, the helper must also continue to set bit V in its router-LSA for the virtual link's transit area. If X was the Designated Router on the segment when the helping relationship began, Y maintains X as the Designated Router until the relationship is terminated.

Router Y enters helper mode when it receives a grace-LSA from X and five checks pass: Y currently has a full adjacency with X over the associated segment; there have been no changes in content to the link-state database, of LS types 1 to 5 and 7, since X restarted; the grace period has not yet expired, meaning the LS age of the grace-LSA is less than the grace period the grace-LSA specifies; local policy allows Y to act as the helper; and Y is not itself in the process of a graceful restart. The RFC gives example policies: never act as a helper, never allow the grace period to exceed a given time, only help on software reloads or upgrades, or never act as a helper for specific routers identified by OSPF Router ID.

Y ceases helping X on a segment when the grace-LSA originated by X is flushed, which indicates a successful termination of the graceful restart; when the grace period expires; or when a change in link-state database contents indicates a network topology change. For that last case the RFC is precise: Y should stop helping when it installs a new LSA with LS types 1 to 5 and 7 whose contents have changed and which would have been flooded to X had Y and X been fully adjacent. A changed AS-external-LSA, for example, does not end the relationship with a neighbour in a stub area, because that neighbour would not see it in any case. An implementation may provide a configuration option to stop link-state database changes from terminating graceful restart, but the RFC warns that this increases the risk of transient routing loops and black holes.

When Y exits helper mode on a segment it reoriginates its LSAs based on the current state of its adjacency to X: it recalculates the Designated Router for the segment, reoriginates its router-LSA for the segment's OSPF area, reoriginates the network-LSA if it is the Designated Router, and reoriginates the router-LSA for the transit area if the segment was a virtual link. A single router may serve as a helper for several restarting neighbours at once, and may help one neighbour on some segments and not on others.
sections.plainLanguage: Each neighbour of the restarting router has a helper role. As long as the network has not changed, the helper keeps mentioning the restarting router in its own link-state advertisements, so other routers keep routing through it. The helper stops as soon as the network changes, the grace period ends, or the restarting router says the restart is over.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility and Unplanned Outages
sections.content:
Backward compatibility with unmodified OSPF routers is an automatic consequence of the functionality documented in this RFC. If one or more neighbours of a router requesting a graceful restart are unmodified, or if they do not receive the grace-LSA, the graceful restart reverts to a normal OSPF restart. The unmodified routers will start routing around the restarted router X as it performs initial database synchronisation, by reissuing their LSAs with links to X omitted. Those LSAs will be interpreted by helper neighbours as a topology change, and by X as an LSA inconsistency, and in either case the result is a return to normal OSPF operation.

The mechanisms can also be used for unplanned outages, such as the crash of a router's control software or an unexpected switchover to a redundant control processor. The RFC warns that attempting a graceful restart after an unplanned outage may not be a good idea, because the router cannot properly prepare for the restart and it seems unlikely that a router could guarantee the sanity of its forwarding tables across an unplanned restart. An implementation that offers the option must allow the network operator to turn it off.

After an unplanned outage the router must originate the grace-LSAs after its control software resumes operation, and they must be originated and sent before the restarted router sends any OSPF Hello packets. On broadcast networks the LSA must be flooded to the AllSPFRouters multicast address, 224.0.0.5, because the restarting router is not aware of its previous DR state. The grace-LSAs are encapsulated in Link State Update packets and sent out to all interfaces, even though the restarted router has no adjacencies and no knowledge of previous adjacencies. An implementation may send them multiple times to improve the probability of delivery. The restart reason in the grace-LSAs must be set to 0, unknown, or 3, switch to redundant control processor, which enables neighbours to decide whether they want to help the router through an unplanned restart.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing has to be changed on the other routers for this to work. If a neighbour does not understand the new messages, it ignores them, stops mentioning the restarting router, and the restart quietly becomes an ordinary one. The RFC also allows the same mechanism after a crash, but warns that a router cannot check its forwarding tables before an unplanned restart, so the operator must be able to switch the feature off.

sections.title: The Grace-LSA Format
sections.content:
The grace-LSA is a link-local scoped Opaque-LSA with an Opaque Type of 3 and an Opaque ID equal to 0. It is originated by a router that wishes to execute a graceful restart of its OSPF software, and it requests that the router's neighbours aid in the restart by continuing to advertise the router as fully adjacent during a specified grace period. Its LS age field is set to 0 when the LSA is first originated, so the current value of the LS age indicates how long ago the restarting router made its request.

The body of the LSA is TLV-encoded, and the format of those TLVs is the same as the format used by the Traffic Engineering Extensions to OSPF. Each TLV has a Type, a Length that gives the length of the value portion in octets, and the value. The TLV is padded to four-octet alignment, and the padding is not included in the length field, so a three octet value has a length of three while the total size of the TLV is eight octets. Nested TLVs are also 32-bit aligned, and unrecognised types are ignored.

Three TLVs can appear in the body of a grace-LSA. The Grace Period (Type=1, length=4) is the number of seconds that the router's neighbours should continue to advertise the router as fully adjacent, regardless of the state of database synchronisation between the router and its neighbours. Because this period began when the grace-LSA's LS age was 0, the grace period terminates when either the LS age of the grace-LSA exceeds the Grace Period value or the grace-LSA is flushed. This TLV must always appear. The Graceful restart reason (Type=2, length=1) encodes the reason as 0 for unknown, 1 for software restart, 2 for software reload or upgrade, or 3 for switch to a redundant control processor, and must also always appear. The IP interface address (Type=3, length=4) is the router's IP interface address on the subnet associated with the grace-LSA, and is required on broadcast, NBMA and Point-to-MultiPoint segments, where the helper uses it to identify the restarting router.

DoNotAge is never set in a grace-LSA, even if the grace-LSA is flooded over a demand circuit, because the LS age field is used to calculate the duration of the grace period. The grace-LSA has link-local scope because it only needs to be seen by the router's direct neighbours. Any additional grace-LSA TLVs must be described in an Internet Draft and will be subject to the expert review of the OSPF Working Group.
sections.plainLanguage: The announcement of a planned restart is a special link-state message with link-local reach. Its body holds a small list of typed items: how long the grace period lasts, why the router is restarting, and, on shared network types, the router's address on that network.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
One of the ways to attack a link-state protocol such as OSPF is to inject false LSAs into, or corrupt existing LSAs in, the link-state database. Injecting a false grace-LSA would allow an attacker to spoof a router that, in reality, has been withdrawn from service. The standard way to prevent such corruption of the link-state database is to secure OSPF protocol exchanges using the cryptographic authentication specified in RFC 2328. An even stronger way of securing link-state database contents has been proposed in RFC 2154.

When cryptographic authentication is used on the restarting router, the preservation of received sequence numbers in non-volatile storage is not mandatory. There is a risk that a replayed Hello packet could cause neighbour state for a deceased neighbour to be created. However, the risk is no greater than during normal operation.
sections.plainLanguage: The main risk is that someone forges the announcement of a planned restart, so that traffic keeps being sent to a router that has really been taken out of service. The RFC says the usual answer applies: protect OSPF exchanges with the cryptographic authentication built into OSPF.

fields.name: LS age
fields.desc: Set to 0 when the LSA is originated; its value shows how long ago the request was made.

fields.name: Advertising Router
fields.desc: The router ID of the restarting router.

fields.name: LS sequence number
fields.desc: The sequence number of the LSA.

fields.name: LS checksum
fields.desc: The Fletcher checksum of the LSA.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the LSA in octets.

viz.caption: THE TLV FORMAT INSIDE A GRACE-LSA (RFC 3623)

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: 1 is the Grace Period, 2 the restart reason, 3 the IP interface address.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the value in octets; padding to four octets is not counted.

fields.name: Value
fields.desc: The value itself, padded to a four-octet boundary.

items.label: UNKNOWN
items.desc: The reason for the restart is not known.

items.label: SOFTWARE RELOAD OR UPGRADE
items.desc: The OSPF software was reloaded or upgraded.

items.label: SWITCH TO REDUNDANT CONTROL PROCESSOR
items.desc: Control moved to a redundant processor.

viz.caption: THE ROLES IN A GRACEFUL RESTART (RFC 3623)

transitions.label: the operator requests a graceful restart
adjacencies re-established, LSA inconsistency or grace period expiry
a grace-LSA arrives from a restarting neighbour
grace-LSA flushed, grace period expired or topology change

viz.caption: WHEN A NEIGHBOUR ENTERS HELPER MODE (RFC 3623)

items.title: Full adjacency
items.text: The neighbour must already have a full adjacency with the restarting router.

items.title: No topology change
items.text: No change to link-state database contents of LS types 1 to 5 and 7 since the restart.

items.title: Grace period running
items.text: The LS age of the grace-LSA must still be below the grace period it carries.

items.title: Local policy
items.text: The configured policy on the neighbour must allow it to act as a helper.

items.title: Not restarting itself
items.text: The neighbour must not be in the middle of its own graceful restart.
